title: Rechargeable battery products are normalized consumer infrastructure while safety and end-of-life systems remain unevenly understood
source_unit: Japan Consumer Affairs Agency, FY2026 Consumer Awareness Survey No. 1: products using lithium-ion batteries, released 17 September 2026
geography: Japan; internet survey of 5,000 people aged 15 and over, quota-allocated by sex, age, and region to population composition, conducted 30 July–3 August 2026

denominator.unit: people aged 15 and over in an internet survey; quota allocation by sex, age, and region

mobile_battery_use.value: More than half of respondents reported currently owning or having previously owned a mobile battery

youngest_ownership.unit: percent of respondents in their teens reporting ownership or prior ownership

oldest_ownership.unit: percent of respondents aged 70 and over reporting ownership or prior ownership

battery_normalization.value: Portable rechargeable power has become ordinary consumer infrastructure, but exposure and experience remain age-stratified

observations.method: Japan Consumer Affairs Agency internet survey of 5,000 people aged 15 and over, with sex, age, and regional quotas aligned to population composition.
observations.uncertainty: Quota internet sampling is not a simple random sample; ownership or prior ownership does not measure frequency, product quality, or actual exposure to battery failure.
observations.subgroup: Japanese respondents aged 15 and over, with reported differences between teens and people aged 70 and over.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower older-adult ownership may reflect different device needs or product substitution rather than lower digital participation or safety vulnerability.

observations.period: July–August 2026; safety awareness and product knowledge

denominator.unit: survey respondents; product-specific usage bases vary

mobile_battery_safety.unit: percent aware that mishandling mobile batteries can cause fires or other accidents

young_adult_safety.unit: percent of respondents in their 20s aware of mobile-battery danger

older_adult_safety.unit: percent of respondents aged 70 and over aware of mobile-battery danger

product_knowledge_gradient.value: Awareness is high for mobile batteries and smartphones but lower for other lithium-ion products such as cordless or robot vacuum cleaners

observations.method: Consumer Affairs Agency survey questions on awareness of fire and accident risks across lithium-ion battery products.
observations.uncertainty: Awareness is self-reported and does not establish correct handling, risk comprehension, or behavior during charging, transport, damage, or disposal.
observations.subgroup: Age groups and users of smartphones, computers, cordless appliances, wearable devices, e-cigarettes, e-bikes, and other battery products.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower awareness of a product category may reflect lower familiarity or different hazard profiles; high awareness can still coexist with routine shortcuts.

observations.period: July–August 2026; price, safety, and performance tradeoffs

denominator.unit: respondents who currently or previously owned a mobile battery; product-specific multiple-response bases also reported

mobile_price_priority.unit: percent citing price as a purchase consideration for mobile batteries

mobile_safety_priority.unit: percent citing safety as a purchase consideration for mobile batteries

other_product_price.unit: percent citing price when purchasing other lithium-ion products

other_product_safety.unit: percent citing safety when purchasing other lithium-ion products

safety_visibility_gap.value: Safety is known as a risk but often ranks below price and performance at purchase, especially outside the most salient mobile-battery category

observations.method: Multiple-response purchase-consideration questions in the Consumer Affairs Agency survey.
observations.uncertainty: Purchase priorities are stated preferences and do not show actual product choices, price elasticity, retailer information, or whether safety standards are trusted.
observations.subgroup: Mobile-battery owners and users of other lithium-ion products, including phones, computers, appliances, e-bikes, and portable power devices.
observations.counterinterpretation: Safety may be treated as a baseline expectation or embedded in brand and certification judgments rather than selected explicitly; low stated salience is not proof of unsafe purchasing.

observations.period: July–August 2026; end-of-life disposal and municipal infrastructure

denominator.unit: mobile-battery owners or former owners asked how they handle an unwanted battery

municipal_rule.unit: percent saying they follow municipal disposal rules

municipal_box.unit: percent saying they use a municipal dedicated collection box

retailer_manufacturer.unit: percent saying they use a retailer or manufacturer take-back service

stored_uncertain.unit: percent saying they keep the battery because they do not know how to dispose of it

age_disposal_gap.value: Storage due to uncertainty was 25.5% among teenagers, while following municipal rules was 43.0% among people aged 70 and over

end_of_life_gap.value: Product safety depends on a disposal and collection system that users can understand and access; household uncertainty can turn a private object into a latent public-safety and waste-management problem

observations.method: Survey question on intended response when a mobile battery is no longer needed, with age-group cross-tabulations.
observations.uncertainty: Responses report intended or remembered disposal behavior and do not measure actual compliance, fire incidents, municipal capacity, or downstream recycling outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Mobile-battery owners and former owners, especially teenagers and people aged 70 and over.
observations.counterinterpretation: Storage can be a cautious response that prevents unsafe disposal, not only evidence of system failure; local rules and access may vary substantially.

related_sources.claim: Consumer Affairs Agency publication page identifying the survey theme, release date, and official PDF.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-technology route from rechargeable-product adoption through age-stratified risk knowledge, price/safety tradeoffs, usage practices, disposal uncertainty, and municipal or take-back infrastructure. It does not establish actual accident rates, unsafe products, causal age effects, disposal compliance, or recycling outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Consumer Affairs Agency PDF reviewed for survey frame, mobile-battery ownership, product-risk awareness, purchase priorities, usage precautions, disposal responses, and age-group contrasts.
